    MA3700 · AIRCRAFT STRUCTURES 1

    Analysis of Thin-Walled Structures

    #Bending in Beams

    Assumptions for bending:

    • Plane section before deformation remains plane after deformation
    • Bending stresses are the dominant normal stresses
    • Material is homogeneous and linearly elastic
    • Deformation is small

    #Conventions and Notations

    Sign conventions and notations:

    • Forces are positive if they are applied in the same direction as the axes
    • Moments are positive if they induce tension in the positive xy quadrant

      Mx​ is positive when it causes the beam to bend upwards (+y-axis)
      My​ is positive when it causes the beam to bend towards +x-axis

    Resolution of bending moments:

    • For θ<90°, both Mx​ and My​ are positive
    • For θ>90°, Mx​ is positive while My​ is negative

    #Symmetrical Bending Theory

    The strain of line ST is,

    εz​=IGST−IG​

    εz​=R dθ(R−y)dθ−R dθ​

    εz​=−Ry​

    εz​=−κy

    The stress is then,

    σz​=Eεz​

    σz​=−Eκy

    Taking moments about the neutral axis,

    ∑MNA​=0

    dM=(σz​ dA)y

    M=∫σz​y dA

    M=−∫Eκy2 dA

    M=−EκINA​

    Note that for a sagging beam, the bending moment is negative and
    the radius of curvature     R, and thus κ, is positive (above the beam).

    Expressing κ as a second order partial derivative,

    💡
    Mx​=−EIxx​∂z2∂2v​

    where EI is known as the flexural rigidity

    Rearranging the stress and moment equations,

    💡
    yσz​​=Ixx​Mx​​=−RE​

    #Example

    The bending moment is resolved into Mx​ and My​.

    The total bending stress is then σz​=Ixx​Mx​y​−Iyy​My​x​.

    Note that Mx​ is a positive bending moment (bends toward positive y-direction)
    and that     My​ is a negative bending moment (bends toward negative x-direction).

    Mx​=100cos30°=86.6 kNm

    My​=100sin30°=50.0 kNm

    Ixx​=12200(300)3​−12175(260)3​=193.7×106 mm4

    Iyy​=2[1220(200)3​]+12260(25)3​=27×106 mm4

    Substituting into the bending stress equation,

    σz​=193.7×106(86.6×106)y​−27×106(50×106)x​

    σz​=0.45y−1.85x

    Note that σz​ is expressed in N/mm2.

    At y=150mm and −100mm≤x≤100mm,

    σz(−100mm)​=0.45(150)−1.85(−100)=252.5 N/mm2

    σz(100mm)​=0.45(150)−1.85(100)=−117.5 N/mm2

    Stress distribution for the upper flange, plotting from left to right.

    At y=−150mm and −100mm≤x≤100mm,

    σz(−100mm)​=0.45(−150)−1.85(−100)=117.5 N/mm2

    σz(100mm)​=0.45(−150)−1.85(100)=−252.5 N/mm2

    Stress distribution for the lower flange, plotting from left to right.

    At the neutral axis, σz​=0.

    0=0.45y−1.85x

    xy​=0.451.85​

    tanα=0.451.85​

    α=76.3°

    #Unsymmetrical Bending Theory

    Consider an arbitrary beam cross-section with an elemental area dA located at a distance x and y
    from the y- and x-axis respectively.

    Stress at any point on the section is,

    σz​=a+bx+cy

    where a, b, and c are constants

    Substituting into the force equilibrium equation,

    Nz​=∫σz​ dA=∫(a+bx+cy) dA=0

    Thus, a=0 since ∫x dA=0 and ∫y dA=0.

    The integrals (first moment of area) are zero since the element is very small.

    Substituting into the moment equilibrium equations,

    Mx​=∫σz​y dA=∫bxy+cy2 dA

    My​=∫σz​x dA=∫bx2+cxy dA

    Since Ixx​=∫y2 dA, Iyy​=∫x2 dA and Ixy​=∫xy dA,

    Mx​=bIxy​+cIxx​

    My​=bIyy​+cIxy​

    Solving the moment equations simultaneously,

    b=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2My​Ixx​−Mx​Ixy​​

    c=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Mx​Iyy​−My​Ixy​​

    Substituting into the bending stress equation,

    σz​=(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2My​Ixx​−Mx​Ixy​​)x+(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Mx​Iyy​−My​Ixy​​)y

    💡
    σz​=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Mx​(Iyy​y−Ixy​x)​+Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2My​(Ixx​x−Ixy​y)​

    If the cross-section of the beam has an axis of symmetry, Ixy​=0.

    💡
    σz​=Ixx​Mx​​y+Iyy​My​​x

    At the neutral axis, σz​=0.

    0=(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2My​Ixx​−Mx​Ixy​​)xNA​+(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Mx​Iyy​−My​Ixy​​)yNA​

    xNA​yNA​​=−Mx​Iyy​−My​Ixy​My​Ixx​−Mx​Ixy​​

    💡
    tanα=−Mx​Iyy​−My​Ixy​My​Ixx​−Mx​Ixy​​

    For a generally applied moment M within the first quadrant,
    Mx​ is a positive moment while My​ is a negative moment.

    #Example

    Position of Centroid

    yˉ​=(120×8)+(80×8)4(120×8)+48(80×8)​=21.6 mm

    xˉ=(120×8)+(80×8)24(120×8)+4(80×8)​=16 mm

    Sectional Properties

    Moment of inertia about x-axis is,

    Ixx​=12120(8)3​+120(8)(17.6)2           +128(80)3​+80(8)(26.4)2

    Ixx​=1.09×106 mm4

    Moment of inertia about y-axis is,

    Iyy​=128(120)3​+120(8)(8)2           +1280(8)3​+80(8)(12)2

    Iyy​=1.31×106 mm4

    Product of inertia is,

    Ixy​=∑(IOxy​+Adx​dy​)i​

    Ixy​=(120×8)(8)(17.6)           +(80×8)(−12)(−26.4)

    Ixy​=0.34×106 mm4

    Note that IOxy​=0 for each rectangular section of the beam since each section
    has an axis of symmetry. Also, the centroid of the vertical section is located on
    the negative     x- and y-axis, thus, dx​ and dy​ for that section are negative.

    Bending Stress

    Subsituting into σz​ and since My​=0,

    σz​=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Mx​(Iyy​y−Ixy​x)​

    σz​=1.09(1.31)−0.3421.5(1.31y−0.34x)​

    σz​=1.5y−0.39x (N/mm2)

    Mx​=1500 Nm

    Mx​=1500000 Nmm

    Mx​=1.5×106 Nmm

    The maximum stresses generally occur at the corners of the beam.

    Top left corner: σz​=1.5(21.6)−0.39(−52)=52.68 N/mm2

    Bottom left corner: σz​=1.5(−66.4)−0.39(−16)=−93.36 N/mm2

    Inclination Angle of Neutral Axis

    At the neutral axis, σz​=0.

    0=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Mx​(Iyy​yNA​−Ixy​xNA​)​

    0=Iyy​yNA​−Ixy​xNA​

    xNA​yNA​​=Iyy​Ixy​​

    tanα=Iyy​Ixy​​

    α=14.24°

    #Shearing in Beams

    Assumptions for shearing:

    • Thin-walled assumptions are valid
    • Effects of axial constraints are neglected
    • Cross-section shape is maintained along the length

    #Transverse Shear Stress

    Consider a cantilever beam being subjected to a load at its free end. Shear flow in the
    beam can be analyzed by cutting the beam at two specific sections — z and z+dz.

    Assuming the beam only experiences pure bending, the load P generates a moment about each section, with the left section experiencing a larger moment due to the additional dz term.

    Analyze a slice of the beam along its length.
    Take summation of forces in the z-direction.

    For an open section beam, there is material
    only on one side of the slice of that beam.

    ∑Fz​=0

    F2​−F1​=H

    (σz​+dσz​)(t ds)−σz​(t ds)=τ(t dz)

    💡
    q=dzdσz​​(t ds)

    Note that shear flow is zero at the open edge
    of the cross-section of an open section beam.

    For a closed section beam, there is material
    on both sides of the slice of that beam.

    ∑Fz​=0

    F2​−F1​=2H

    (σz​+dσz​)(2t ds)−σz​(2t ds)=τ(2t dz)

    💡
    q=dzdσz​​(t ds)

    #Relating Bending to Shear

    Consider an arbitrary shaped thin-walled beam subjected to a varying distributed load. Shear stress is uniform across the thickness at any location in the wall.

    ∑MA​=0

    (p dz)(21​dz)+Mx​+Sy​ dz=Mx​+∂z∂Mx​​dz

    21​p(dz)2+Sy​ dz=∂z∂Mx​​dz

    21​p dz+Sy​=∂z∂Mx​​

    💡
    ∂z∂Mx​​=Sy​

    Note that since dz is small, the moment due to P can be considered to be negligible.

    Consider force equilibrium of an element dz of thickness t from the thin-walled beam.

    ∑Fz​=0

    σz​(t ds)+q(dz)=(σz​+∂z∂σz​​dz)t ds+(q+∂s∂q​ds)dz

    0=∂z∂σz​​t dsdz+∂s∂q​dsdz

    💡
    ∂s∂q​=−t∂z∂σz​​

    Differentiating the bending stress equation with respect to z,

    σz​=Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Mx​(Iyy​y−Ixy​x)​+Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2My​(Ixx​x−Ixy​y)​

    ∂z∂σz​​=∂z∂Mx​​(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Iyy​y−Ixy​x​)+∂z∂My​​(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Ixx​x−Ixy​y​)

    ∂z∂σz​​=Sy​(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Iyy​y−Ixy​x​)+Sx​(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Ixx​x−Ixy​y​)

    Integrating the above equation with respect to s,

    ∫0s​∂q=−∫0s​t∂z∂σz​​ ∂s

    💡
    qs​−q0​=−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sy​Iyy​−Sx​Ixy​​)∫0s​yt ds−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sx​Ixx​−Sy​Ixy​​)∫0s​xt ds

    For an open section beam, q0​=0 at the open edge of the cross section.
    For a closed section beam,     q0​ at s=0 is unknown.

    If the cross-section of the beam has an axis of symmetry, Ixy​=0.

    💡
    qs​−q0​=−Ixx​Sy​​∫0s​yt ds−Iyy​Sx​​∫0s​xt ds

    Note that the equation for transverse shear is derived from the bending stress equation.
    Thus, the location of the neutral axis of the section needs to be determined first.

    #Shear Center of Open Section

    The shear center is defined as the point in the cross-section through which shear loads produce no twisting. Thus, when a shear load is applied through the shear center, a
    bending stress is produced and shear stress is uniform across the wall thickness.

    Any shear load may be represented as a combination of the shear load applied through
    the shear center and a torque due to that same shear load. The stresses produced by
    each can be summed up using superposition.

    Suppose shear center R lies somewhere along the axis
    of symmetry of an open section beam, and an arbitrary shear load Sy​ is applied through R.

    Thus, Ixy​=0, q0​=0, and Sx​=0.
    The shear flow of the beam is then,

    qs​=−Ixx​Sy​​∫0s​yt ds

    The moment of inertia about the x-axis is,

    Ixx​=12th3​+2[12bt3​+bt(2h​)2]

    Ixx​=12th3​+2bth2​

    Ixx​=12th3​(1+h6b​)

    The higher-order t3-term is considered to be negligible.

    The upper flange is located y=2h​ from R.

    qflange​=−Ixx​Sy​​(2h​)t∫0s​ds

    qflange​=−h2(1+6b/h)6Sy​​s

    The shear flow for the lower flange will result in the
    same equation but with     y=−2h​ instead. Note that
    the sign indicates the slope of the shear distribution
    in the direction of     s.

    For the web, y=2h​−s.

    qweb​=qB​−Ixx​Sy​​t∫0s​(2h​−s) ds

    qweb​=qB​−Ixx​Sy​t​(2hs​−2s2​)

    Note that shear flow for the web begins at the
    shear flow value at point     B, thus the first term.

    Taking summation of moments about A,

    dM=2h​(qflange​ds)+2h​(qflange​ds)

    M=h∫0b​qflange​ ds

    Sy​⋅e=h(h2(1+6b/h)6Sy​​)∫0b​s ds

    Sy​⋅e=h(1+6b/h)6Sy​​[2s2​]0b​

    💡
    e=h(1+6b/h)3b2​

    #Shear Center of Closed Section

    For a closed section, the shear flow can be determined by first analyzing the equivalent loading on an open section, which is the basic shear flow, followed by determining the
    value of q0​.

    qs​−q0​=−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sy​Iyy​−Sx​Ixy​​)∫0s​yt ds−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sx​Ixx​−Sy​Ixy​​)∫0s​xt ds

    qs​−q0​=qb​

    💡
    qs​=qb​+q0​

    where qb​ represents the basic shear flow (shear flow assuming an open section)

    If the applied shear forces Sx​ and Sy​ act through the shear center, there should be zero twist in the section.

    ϕ=2A0​G1​∮tqs​​ ds=0

    0=∮t1​(qb​+q0​) ds

    0=∮tqb​​ ds+q0​∮t1​ ds

    💡
    q0​=−∮ds/t∮(qb​/t) ds​

    If the applied shear forces Sx​ and Sy​ do not act through the shear center,

    Sx​y−Sy​x=∮rqs​ ds

    Sx​y−Sy​x=∮r(qb​+q0​) ds

    Sx​y−Sy​x=∮rqb​ ds+∮rq0​ ds

    Sx​y−Sy​x=∮rqb​ ds+2A0​q0​

    💡
    q0​=2A0​Sx​y−Sy​x−∮rqb​ ds​

    When shear forces do not act through the shear center, it results in a torque about the
    shear center. Thus, the problem can be broken down into shear flow due to the vertical
    shear force and shear flow due to torsion. Hence, the second term     2A0​q0​.

    After obtaining q0​, the location of the shear center can be determined by taking
    summation of moments of the shear flow in the section about a chosen point.

    #Example 1

    Section has axis of symmetry about x, thus Ixy​=0.
    Also, no shear force in the x-direction, thus Sx​=0.

    qs​−q0​=−Ixx​Sy​​∫0s​yt ds

    qb​=−25.78×1061×106​∫0s​yt ds

    qb​=−0.03879∫0s​yt ds

    Note that q0​ is unknown.

    Analyzing as an open section

    Cut the section at A and analyze as an open section.

    Shear flow values obtained will contribute to qb​.

    Shear flow in AFE is,

    qbAFE​​=−0.03879(3)∫0s​(125−s) ds

    qbAFE​​=−0.11637(125s−21​s2)

    Note that shear flow distribution is parabolic.

    Shear flow in ED is,

    qbED​​=−0.03879(3)∫0s​−125 ds

    qbED​​=14.546s

    Note that shear flow distribution is linear.

    Shear flow at D is,

    qbD​​=14.546(150)=2182 N/mm

    Note that shear flow does not begin at zero.

    Shear flow in DCB is,

    qbDCB​​=qbD​​−0.03879(6)∫0s​−(125−s) ds

    qbDCB​​=2182+0.23274(125s−21​s2)

    Note that shear flow distribution is parabolic with an additional uniform shear flow distribution added.

    Shear flow in BA is,

    qbBA​​=qbB​​−0.03879(3)∫0s​125 ds

    qbBA​​=2182−14.546s

    Note that shear flow distribution is linear.

    Shear flow distribution

    q0​=−∮ds/t∮(qb​/t) ds​

    ∮tqb​​ ds=∫3qbAFE​​​+3qbED​​​+6qbDCB​​​+3qbBA​​​ ds

    ∮t1​ ds=∫3250​+3150​+6250​+3150​=225

    Integrating for AFE,

    31​∫qbAFE​​ ds=31​∫0250​−0.11637(125s−21​s2)

    31​∫qbAFE​​ ds=−0.03879[62.5s2−61​s3]0250​

    31​∫qbAFE​​ ds=−50508 N/mm

    Negative sign indicates that shear flow is clockwise direction.

    Integrating for ED,

    31​∫qbED​​ ds=31​∫0150​14.546s ds

    31​∫qbED​​ ds=54547.5 N/mm

    Positive value indicates shear flow is anticlockwise direction.

    Integrating for DCB,

    61​∫qbDCB​​ ds=61​∫0250​2182+0.23274(125s−21​s2) ds

    61​∫qbDCB​​ ds=61​[2182s+14.546s2−0.03879s3]0250​

    61​∫qbDCB​​ ds=141422 N/mm

    Positive value indicates shear flow is anticlockwise direction.

    Integrating for BA,

    31​∫qbBA​​ ds=31​∫0150​2182−14.546s ds

    31​∫qbBA​​ ds=31​[2182s−7.273s2]0150​

    31​∫qbBA​​ ds=54552.5 N/mm

    Positive value indicates shear flow is anticlockwise direction.

    q0​=−225−50508+54547.5+141422+54552.5​

    q0​=−889 N/mm

    Shear center

    Taking summation of moments about E,

    Sy​ex​=−250F1​+250F2​+150F3​

    Using similar triangles,

    b1293.6​=150−b889.4​

    b=89 mm

    a=61 mm

    Shear Forces

    F1​=21​(61)(889.4)=27126.7 N

    F2​=21​(89)(1293.6)=57565.2 N

    F3​=1293.6(250)+32​(1819)(250)=626566.7 N

    Substituting into the moment equation,

    ex​=1×106−250(27126.7)+250(57565.2)+150(626566.7)​

    ex​=102 mm

    #Example 2

    #Part (a)

    Section has axis of symmetry about x and y, thus Ixy​=0.
    Also, there is no shear force in the x-direction, thus Sx​=0.

    Ixx​=2[124(150)3​]+2[12100(4)3​+(100×4)(75)2]

    Ixx​=6.75×106 mm4

    Note that the higher order t3-term is considered negligible.

    qs​−q0​=−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sy​Iyy​−Sx​Ixy​​)∫0s​yt ds−(Ixx​Iyy​−Ixy​2Sx​Ixx​−Sy​Ixy​​)∫0s​xt ds

    qs​−q0​=−Ixx​Sy​​∫0s​yt ds

    qs​−q0​=−6.75×10610000(4)​∫0s​y ds

    qb​=−0.0059259∫0s​y ds

    Analyzing as an open section

    Shear flow in AB is,

    qAB​=−0.0059259∫0s​75 ds

    qAB​=−0.0059259(75s)

    qAB​=−0.44444s

    Shear flow in AB is in the clockwise direction.

    Shear flow at B is,

    qB​=−0.44444(100)

    qB​=−44.444 N/mm

    Shear flow in BC is,

    qBC​=qB​−0.0059259∫0s​(75−s) ds

    qBC​=−44.444−0.0059259(75s−21​s2)

    Shear flow in BC is in the clockwise direction.

    Shear flow in CD is,

    qCD​=qC​−0.0059259∫0s​−75 ds

    qCD​=−44.444+0.0059259(75s)

    qCD​=−44.444+0.44444s

    Shear flow in CD is in the clockwise direction.

    Shear flow in DA is,

    qDA​=−0.0059259∫0s​−(75−s) ds

    qDA​=0.0059259(75s−21​s2)

    qDA​=0.44444s−0.002963s2

    Shear flow in DA is in the anticlockwise direction.

    Shear flow distribution

    Since the shear force does not act through the shear center,

    q0​=2A0​Sx​y−Sy​x−∮rqb​ ds​

    q0​=2A0​−Sy​x−∮rqb​ ds​

    where ∮rqb​ ds is the internal moment of qb​

    Taking moments about O,

    2A0​q0​=−10000(60)−∮rqb​ ds

    2A0​q0​=−600000−∮rqb​ ds

    Assuming anticlockwise moments as positive,

    ∮rqb​ ds=−75FAB​−75FCD​−50FBC​+50FDA​

    ∮rqb​ ds=−150FAB​−50FBC​+50FDA​

    FAB​=∫0s​qAB​ ds=∫0100​−0.44444s ds

    FAB​=[−0.22222s2]0100​

    FAB​=−2222.2 N

    FBC​=∫0s​qBC​ ds=∫0150​−44.444−0.0059259(75s−21​s2) ds

    FBC​=[−44.444s−0.22222s2+0.00098765]0150​

    FBC​=−8333 N

    FDA​=∫0s​qDA​ ds=∫0150​0.44444s−0.002963s2 ds

    FDA​=[0.22222s2−0.00098765s3]0150​

    FDA​=1667 N

    ∮rqb​ ds=−150(2222.2)−50(8333)+50(1667)

    ∮rqb​ ds=−666630 Nmm

    Note that the direction (sign) of the forces have been accounted for in
    the initial equation. Thus, only the magnitude of the forces are required.

    2A0​q0​=−600000−∮rqb​ ds

    2(100×150)q0​=−600000−(−666630)

    q0​=2.221 N/mm

    Since value of q0​ is positive, shear flow is in the anticlockwise direction.

    #Part (b)

    Total shear flow can be resolved into qtorque​ and qvert​.
    qtorque​ can be determined using Bredt-Batho theory. (shear flow due to torque)
    qvert​ can be determined using qs​=qb​+q0​. (shear flow in a closed section)

    Shear Flow due to Torque

    T=2Am​qtorque​

    Sy​x=2Am​qtorque​

    qtorque​=2(100×150)10000(60)​

    qtorque​=20 N/mm

    Shear Flow due to Shear Force

    Since the section is symmetrical about both axis, shear center lies on the centroid of the section.

    With the shear force acting through the shear
    center, shear flow in the vertical sections will
    be in the same direction as the shear force.

    Also, shear flow in the horizontal sections will emanate from the y-axis of symmetry, such
    that q=0 at that axis.

    qs​−q0​=−0.0059259∫0s​y ds

    qs​=−0.0059259∫0s​y ds

    Note that ds begins at the y-axis of symmetry, thus q0​=0.

    Shear flow in 0B is,

    q0B​=−0.0059259∫0s​75 ds

    q0B​=−0.44444s

    Shear flow in BC is,

    qBC​=qB​−0.0059259∫0s​(75−s) ds
